brief.outcome: Bring the returns rate on the women's clothing store from 31% to under 20% by March 2027, by finding the real reasons for returns and fixing product pages, size charts and the returns form, without touching the free returns policy before February.

ambition.goal_beyond: Profit per order rises because fewer garments come back, and the store keeps knowing why the ones that do come back are returned.
rungs: Update size charts and product pages so fewer sizing returns happen
Find the real reasons behind the returns (including the 60% with no reason) by product and SKU, and fix each product's biggest cause, sizing or not
Keep it true: a monthly returns check by product and reason, with a returns form that always captures a usable reason, that flags a rising product early
ambition.judge: Shopify returns report (physical returns by SKU) on one written definition, plus reasons recorded by the operations lead on a sample of at least 100 physical returned units, which does not depend on what customers typed in the form

brief.deliverable: A trusted returns baseline, real reasons by product, the chosen product page, size chart and returns form changes prepared and applied by wave, and a monthly readout against 20%
done: The 31% recomputed on a written definition from Shopify returns and orders
Real reasons found for the blank-reason returns from a sample of returned units
Every cause hypothesis marked supported, refuted or unknown, with numbers
Owner and operations lead chose the fixes and the reasons are recorded
Size chart, page and returns form changes prepared, reviewed and applied by product wave
Return rate read monthly against 20% with conversion and rating checked
Learnings and a monthly watch rule saved
guardrails: The free returns policy is not changed before February
Conversion rate on changed product pages does not fall more than 5% (relative) against unchanged products
Average product rating in Judge.me does not fall
Return shipping cost per return stays near Rs 180 or lower

Shopify access is read-only for us: the owner or operations lead makes every change
Working data stays in files in this project (we chose this because the owner asked us to choose)

answers.question: What store and how big?
answers.answer: Women's clothing on Shopify, about 1,800 orders a month

answers.question: How big is the problem?
answers.answer: Return rate 31% over the last quarter (Shopify returns report); 60% of returns have the reason field blank; return shipping costs about Rs 180 per return

answers.question: What does the owner think and want?
answers.answer: Thinks sizing is the main reason; wants returns under 20% by March

answers.question: What can change?
answers.answer: Product pages, size charts and the returns form; not the free returns policy before February

answers.question: Tools, data home, decisions?
answers.answer: Shopify MCP read access; reviews in Judge.me as a CSV export; choose where to keep data; the owner decides with the operations lead

research.approach: Practitioners first pin down what the return rate counts, because Shopify separates physically returned quantity from every reversed quantity (refunds, cancellations, edits), and a rate on the wrong one points at the wrong fix. They then get the true reasons from the rawest source, the returned units and notes, because customer-selected reasons are missing or vague, split returns by product and SKU, and compare the reasoned returns with what reviews say about fit and quality. Fixes are made by product wave so unchanged products act as the comparison. The returns form is rebuilt to capture a usable reason, since without one the next round of analysis is blind.

sources.title: Self-serve returns setup (Shopify Help Center)
sources.note: Platform documentation, page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03. Return reasons offered depend on the product category (for apparel, options such as too big or too small) and customers can add a note for the store.

sources.title: Sales report (Shopify Help Center)
sources.note: Platform documentation, page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03. Defines the return line item reason, returned quantity (units physically returned) and reversed quantity (also includes refunds, cancellations and edits).

sources.title: 2025 Retail Returns Landscape (NRF and Happy Returns)
sources.note: Industry research published 2025-10-15: an estimated 19.3% of online sales returned in 2025 across large US retailers, and 82% of consumers call free returns important. Useful as a yardstick for the 20% target; apparel runs higher than the all-product average and the survey is of large merchants.

sources.title: Exporting reviews (Judge.me Help Center)
sources.note: Vendor documentation, page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03. The CSV has review text, rating, date, product ID and handle, but not SKUs, order details or verified status, so reviews are matched to SKUs through the product handle.

steps.name: Write down what the return rate counts and recompute it
steps.why: Shopify separates returned quantity from reversed quantity; the 31% could mix physical returns with cancellations and refunds.

steps.name: Split returns by product, SKU, size and order type
steps.why: Returns usually concentrate in a few products; each needs its own fix, and bracketing orders look different from single-size orders.

steps.name: Get the real reasons from the returned units
steps.why: The form reason is blank on 60% and customer-chosen labels are coarse; inspecting returned units gives the true reason and size.

steps.name: Read the reviews for fit, fabric and expectation mismatches
steps.why: Reviews say why garments did not work, but the CSV lacks SKUs and only covers people who kept the item.

steps.name: Test the causes and size what each costs
steps.why: Cost per return and the share each cause explains decide which fix comes first.

steps.name: Fix the returns form, size charts and pages by product wave
steps.why: Changing products in waves lets unchanged products serve as the comparison; a better form feeds every later round.

steps.name: Read returns by order cohort, after returns have had time to arrive
steps.why: Returns arrive days or weeks after the order, so a recent cohort looks better than it is until it matures.

pitfalls.text: Treating the owner's 'sizing' belief as fact when the reason field is blank on 60% of returns; the blank group may differ from the filled one.
Computing the rate on reversed quantity, which includes cancellations and edits, and chasing a problem that is partly not returns at all.
Using reviews alone: they miss the buyers who returned the item and the CSV has no SKU or order data.
Judging a fix on recent orders before their returns have arrived.

stages.name: Pin down the returns problem
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured problem, a target, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Gather orders, returns and reviews
stages.goal: Pull six months of orders, line items, returns and refunds, and the Judge.me reviews matched to products, into CSV files in this project.

checks.name: Order and return counts match Shopify's own totals for the same dates within 1%
At least 95% of reviews are matched to a product by handle, and the rest are listed
The share of returns with a blank reason is recomputed and compared with the reported 60%

stages.name: Log the real reasons on returned units
stages.goal: The operations lead logs every returned unit for 2 to 3 weeks with size ordered, the customer's reason if any, condition and a short fit or defect note, to learn why the blank returns come back.

checks.name: At least 100 returned units are logged, or the shortfall is stated and findings marked low-confidence
Every row has the SKU, size ordered and a reason found on inspection or marked unknown
Units are logged as they arrive, not picked, and the logging period is stated

stages.name: Check the 31% means what we think
stages.goal: Write the definition of return rate, recompute it on physical returns and on all reversals, profile the blank-reason returns, and check how returns are created.

outputs.name: Return rate definition and baseline check

checks.name: The rate is recomputed three ways (orders returned, units returned, value returned) on physical returns, and the reported 31% is matched to one of them or the gap is explained
Cancellations, refused deliveries and refunds without a returned item are counted separately
Blank-reason returns are split by who created them (customer or staff), product and month
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and the baseline to use for the target

stages.name: Find why clothes come back
stages.goal: Test the hypotheses by product and SKU against reasons, the returned-unit log and reviews. Size what each cause costs. Keep competing explanations.

checks.name: Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN, with the numbers behind it
A product finding rests on at least 30 orders of that product, otherwise it is marked low-confidence
The sizing belief is tested separately on reasoned returns, the returned-unit log and reviews, and all three results are shown
Each cause is costed in rupees a month (return shipping, refund handling, written-off stock) and ranked
Each main finding names at least one competing explanation

stages.name: Rank the fixes
stages.goal: Turn supported findings into a ranked list of fixes by product wave, each with expected returns avoided, saving in rupees, effort, confidence, risk to conversion and how it will be measured.

checks.name: Every option cites the finding it rests on
Every option has returns avoided, rupee saving, effort, confidence, risk and how it will be measured
No option changes the free returns policy before February
The options together are sized against the 11-point gap to 20%, and the shortfall is stated

stages.name: Owner and operations lead choose
stages.goal: The owner and the operations lead pick the fixes, the product waves and their order. Ask for the reason when they pass over the top option and record it.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over options are in decisions.jsonl
A reason is recorded wherever the top option was passed over

stages.name: Prepare the fixes
stages.goal: Prepare the chosen changes: a returns form whose reasons are specific (including how much too big or small), size charts with garment measurements, fit notes and page text for each product in wave 1, ready to apply. Batch into one review.

checks.name: Only chosen changes are included, and none touches the free returns policy
Every size chart figure is a garment measurement supplied by the owner or operations lead, not an estimate
The returns form makes a reason required and offers specific choices plus a free note, and the old reason list is mapped to the new
Page text uses buyer words from reviews and makes no promise the garment cannot keep

stages.optional_when: No page, chart or form change was chosen.

stages.name: Apply the fixes by product wave
stages.goal: The owner or operations lead applies the returns form change and wave 1 product changes, leaves comparable products unchanged for now, and logs each change date. Register the comparison before wave 1 goes live.

checks.name: The wave comparison (changed products versus similar unchanged products, same period) is registered in experiments.jsonl before wave 1 goes live
Every change has the date and time it was made
A test return is made through the new form and the reason is recorded in Shopify

stages.name: Read the returns honestly
stages.goal: Each month read return rate by order cohort on the written definition, for changed versus unchanged products, with conversion, rating and cost per return checked.

checks.name: Only order cohorts at least 30 days old are called, or the cohort is marked immature
The same definition, product mix and months are used for changed versus unchanged products and for the baseline
Conversion on changed pages, rating and return shipping cost per return are checked every read
A product group is called better or worse only with at least 100 orders in each group; otherwise INCONCLUSIVE

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Close the comparison, record which fixes cut returns, and propose a monthly returns watch by product and reason; plan wave 2 and the February policy conversation with real numbers.

checks.name: Every registered comparison is closed in experiments.jsonl
Each proposed rule says whether it holds for this product, this store or the playbook

hypotheses.statement: The 31% counts more than physical returns (cancellations, refused deliveries or refunds without a returned item), so the real return rate is lower.
hypotheses.test: Recompute the rate on returned quantity (physical) and on reversed quantity (all reversals) for the same quarter.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The physical-return rate is 5 points or more below 31%.
hypotheses.refute_if: The physical-return rate is within 2 points of 31%.

hypotheses.statement: Sizing and fit are the main reason for returns.
hypotheses.test: Share of too-big and too-small among reasoned returns, the share of fit complaints in the returned-unit log, and fit mentions in reviews by product.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Fit reasons are 40% or more of reasoned returns and of the logged units, and reviews of the top returned products mention fit on 15% or more of reviews.
hypotheses.refute_if: Fit is under 20% in the returned-unit log.

hypotheses.statement: The returns with a blank reason differ from those with a reason (for example, staff-created returns or one set of products), so the reasoned 40% misleads.
hypotheses.test: Compare blank and reasoned returns by creator, product and month, and compare the reasons found on inspection for blank returns with the stated reasons.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Blank returns are 80% or more staff-created, or their inspected reasons differ from the stated mix by 15 points or more on any main reason.
hypotheses.refute_if: Blank and reasoned returns share the same product, creator and reason mix within 10 points.

hypotheses.statement: A small number of products or SKUs cause most of the returns.
hypotheses.test: Returns and return rate by SKU, ranked, with the cumulative share.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The top 10 SKUs hold 40% or more of returns, with a return rate 10 points or more above the store average.
hypotheses.refute_if: Returns are spread so that the top 10 SKUs hold under 20%.

hypotheses.statement: Customers order the same item in two sizes and send one back.
hypotheses.test: Orders with two or more sizes of the same product and their return rate against single-size orders.
hypotheses.confirm_if: These orders are 10% or more of orders and return at least 40%, making them 15% or more of returns.

hypotheses.statement: Quality, colour or fabric not matching the page is a second cause besides fit.
hypotheses.test: Share of not-as-described, defective or colour reasons in the returned-unit log, and fabric or colour complaints in reviews.
hypotheses.confirm_if: These are 20% or more of logged units, or a product has such complaints in 10% or more of its reviews.
hypotheses.refute_if: They are under 10% of logged units and rare in reviews.

measurement.window: From the first applied change to March 2027, read monthly by order cohort once the cohort is at least 30 days old; compare changed products with similar unchanged products in the same months.
measurement.min_volume: At least 100 orders in each compared product group; fewer is INCONCLUSIVE.
measurement.stop_rule: Pause a product change and ask the owner and operations lead if conversion on changed pages falls more than 5% (relative) against unchanged products or the rating falls.
